title: Settling disputes
hookLine: after a teacher's death disputes arise; seven ways of settling them

lines: A TEACHER DIES. HIS FOLLOWERS SPLIT.
cards: A young novice named Cunda has spent the rains in the town of Pāvā, and he walks in with bad news.
A well-known teacher of the time has just died there, and his followers are already splitting into camps, wounding each other with words: you don't understand the teaching; I do.
Cunda tells Ānanda, and Ānanda takes him straight to the Buddha. Ānanda is worried. When you're gone, he asks, could this happen to us?

teach.b: The Buddha's answer is reassuring and sharp at once. Disputes about small things, how monks earn their keep, details of the monastic rules, those are minor, Ānanda.

A dispute about the path itself would be serious, and would harm many. Then he lays out how to settle the disputes that will come. The Pali word for a dispute is adhikaraṇa, and the sutta gives seven ways to settle one.

teach.h: FACE TO FACE, BY VOTE, BY ADMISSION.
teach.b: Some you'd expect: face to face, with the people, the teaching and the rules all present; by majority vote, when nothing else works; by someone's own admission of what they did. Some are surprisingly humane.
One clears a monk accused of something he did while out of his mind: he's not held responsible.

teach.h: CLEARED BY MEMORY, OR BY PAST MADNESS.
teach.b: One clears a monk with a clear memory and a clean record, so false accusations don't stick.
And the last has a striking name: covering over with grass.

When a whole community is tangled in a long, messy quarrel, with faults on every side, and digging it all up would only make things worse, both sides agree to set it aside together, like covering mud with grass so people can walk again.
Serious offenses are excluded. For the rest, peace is allowed to matter more than a full accounting.
Then six qualities that keep a community warm: kindness in body, speech and mind, sharing what you receive, the same good conduct, and the same understanding.
Disputes will come; a community can be built to settle them.

how: The seven ways of settling disputes (adhikaraṇa-samatha) are part of the monastic code recited at the fortnightly Pāṭimokkha ceremony, and monastic communities still use them, including 'covering over with grass', to resolve conflicts.

games.q: your community is tangled in a long quarrel with faults on every side. digging it all up would make it worse. what's the seventh way?
o: cover it over with grass: agree together to set it aside
wait for the teacher to decide
games.why: both sides agree to let it rest, like covering mud with grass so people can walk again. serious offenses are excluded.

practice: Bring to mind one small, ongoing friction: whose turn it is, a comment that stung, an old disagreement that keeps resurfacing.

Ask which of the seven ways might fit: face to face, an honest admission, or covering it over with grass, agreeing together to let it rest. Picture the first sentence you'd say, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Settling disputes. The seven ways the Buddha gave his community, from face to face to covering over with grass, so a quarrel doesn't outlive its cause.

orig.note: Pali adhikaraṇa: a dispute or legal issue in the community. the seven ways are the adhikaraṇa-samathas.

carryVoice: Your line: settle it. Even a long quarrel can be covered with grass. Day four hundred eighty, done.
